beats.headline: Why does your database roll back perfectly valid writes?
beats.subline: It isn't a bug—it is the ACID guarantee keeping your financial data sane.
beats.narration: Ever wonder why a database rejects a perfectly valid update? It is likely an ACID constraint. If your code crashes mid-transaction, you need a guarantee that money doesn't just vanish into thin air.

beats.title: The Transaction Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: From BEGIN to COMMIT
beats.narration: Atomicity means all-or-nothing. Consistency enforces schema rules like CHECK constraints. Isolation manages concurrency, and Durability uses a Write-Ahead Log to ensure your data survives even a total power loss.

beats.title: Schema-Level Invariants

steps.explanation: The database rejects the update before it hits disk if the balance drops below zero.
If the second update fails, the first is rolled back automatically.

beats.narration: Never trust the application layer to enforce business rules alone. By putting a CHECK constraint directly in the schema, you prevent invalid states even if your Java code has a logic bug.

beats.title: Isolation Levels
beats.narration: Most engines default to Read Committed, which is fast. But for complex multi-row financial invariants, you might need Serializable isolation to prevent subtle race conditions.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Schema constraints are your first line of defense

beats.narration: That's the ACID foundation. In Part 2, we tackle normalization and why denormalizing historical facts is actually a best practice.

beats.headline: Is your database schema causing silent data corruption?
beats.subline: Over-normalization is a trap. Here is when to break the rules.
beats.narration: Normalization prevents anomalies, but it can also ruin your historical reporting. If you join to current prices for past orders, you are corrupting your own financial records.

beats.title: The Historical Fact Pattern

steps.explanation: Store the price at the moment of purchase. Never rely on the current product catalog price.

beats.narration: This is a deliberate denormalization. By saving the unit price at purchase, you ensure that even if the product price changes tomorrow, your historical order totals remain accurate.

beats.title: Normalization Stages
beats.narration: 1NF requires atomic values. 3NF removes transitive dependencies—like storing a city and state based on a zip code. 3NF is your default, but always snapshot historical facts.

beats.title: When to Denormalize
beats.subtitle: Performance vs. Consistency
beats.narration: If your dashboard queries are timing out, denormalize by creating a materialized view. The cost is maintenance—you must keep that data in sync with the source of truth.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: 3NF is the standard for data integrity
Always snapshot prices for historical orders
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): B-Tree internals and the Leftmost Prefix Rule →
beats.narration: That covers modeling. In Part 3, we dive into B-Trees and why your composite index might be completely ignored by the query planner.

beats.headline: Why is your composite index being ignored?
beats.subline: It's the Leftmost Prefix Rule. If you miss the first column, the index is dead.
beats.narration: You built a composite index, but the query planner is still doing a sequential scan. It's likely you violated the Leftmost Prefix Rule. Let's see how B-Trees actually traverse your data.

beats.title: B-Tree Traversal
beats.subtitle: O(log n) search efficiency
beats.narration: B-Trees keep keys sorted. The root narrows the range, branches refine it, and leaves point to the actual row. If your query doesn't start with the first indexed column, the engine can't use the tree.

beats.title: Composite Index Strategy
beats.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_status_created
    ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

steps.explanation: Must filter by tenant_id first. status and created_at only work if tenant_id is included.
Put equality columns before range columns for maximum selectivity.

beats.narration: Always put equality columns before range columns. If you filter by created_at first, the B-Tree loses its ability to group status values, forcing a scan.

beats.title: Index Optimizations
beats.narration: Covering indexes let you fetch data directly from the index leaf. Partial indexes are even better—they only index the rows you actually care about, keeping the tree small and fast.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Leftmost prefix is mandatory for B-Trees
Equality columns go before range columns
Partial indexes save RAM and write I/O
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans →
beats.narration: That's indexing. In Part 4, we stop guessing and start reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE plans to see exactly why a query is slow.

beats.headline: Why is your query slow even with an index?
beats.subline: Stop guessing. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals the truth behind the execution plan.
beats.narration: You added an index, but the query is still slow. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is your only source of truth. Let's decode the plan and find the bottleneck.

beats.title: Reading the Plan
beats.caption: The 4 signals that matter

lines.text: Index Scan using idx_orders on orders

beats.narration: If you see 'Rows Removed by Filter', your index is failing to narrow the search. High 'shared read' counts mean you're hitting the disk, not the RAM cache.

beats.title: Scan Types
beats.subtitle: Choosing the right strategy
beats.narration: Seq Scans are fine for small tables, but deadly for large ones. Index Only Scans are the gold standard—they never touch the main table heap.

beats.title: Planner Estimates
beats.narration: If estimates are way off, the planner will choose a terrible join strategy. Run ANALYZE to refresh column histograms and keep your plans efficient.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
takeaways: Buffers: shared hit = RAM, shared read = Disk
Stale stats lead to poor join paths

beats.narration: That's performance profiling. In Part 5, we wrap up with CTEs and Window Functions for complex analytical reporting.

beats.headline: Stop writing nested subqueries from hell.
beats.subline: CTEs and Window Functions make your analytics readable and performant.
beats.narration: Nested subqueries are unreadable. CTEs let you define a clear pipeline, and Window Functions compute aggregates without collapsing your rows. Let's finish the series.

beats.title: Pipeline with CTEs

steps.explanation: Names the intermediate step, creating a readable top-to-bottom flow.

beats.narration: CTEs turn complex logic into a readable pipeline. In modern PostgreSQL, they are inlined by default, so you get the readability of a subquery with the performance of a join.

beats.title: Window Functions
beats.code:
SELECT 
    salary,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk
FROM employees;

steps.explanation: Computes the rank per department without collapsing the rows into a single group.

beats.narration: Window functions are powerful. They calculate rankings or running totals while keeping every row in your result set. Use PARTITION BY to reset the calculation per group.

beats.title: Ranking Ties
beats.narration: Use RANK when you need to respect gaps, and DENSE_RANK when you want a continuous sequence. Both are essential for top-N reporting.
